summary:
PeatLens is an interactive Earth system research website that helps users investigate historical environmental trends in peatland ecosystems using NASA Earth observation data.

Focusing on Kuala Baram, Sarawak, as its initial case study, PeatLens integrates NASA GPM, MODIS, and SMAP datasets to explore changes in rainfall, land surface temperature, vegetation conditions, and model-estimated groundwater levels.

Through interactive maps, educational peatland illustrations, and time-series visualizations, users can explore environmental changes across different periods. Seasonal Mann–Kendall tests and Sen’s slope estimates help distinguish short-term fluctuations from statistically significant long-term trends. Historical NASA FIRMS thermal anomaly records provide additional environmental context.

By transforming complex satellite data into accessible visualizations and evidence-based interpretations, PeatLens supports environmental education, scientific curiosity, and greater awareness of peatland changes.

Rather than predicting fires, PeatLens encourages users to investigate environmental trends, compare evidence, and understand scientific uncertainty.
details:
PeatLens: Investigating Peatland Trends with NASA Earth Data

1. Project Overview

PeatLens is an interactive Earth system research website designed to help users explore and understand historical environmental trends in peatland ecosystems by leveraging NASA Earth observation data.

Focusing on Kuala Baram in Sarawak as its initial case study, the project utilizes interactive maps, environmental data visualizations, and statistical analysis to transform complex Earth science data into accessible, understandable information. This enables non-specialist users to investigate environmental trends without the need for complex data processing or statistical computation.

2. Problem & Motivation

Peatlands are vital ecosystems that play a critical role in carbon storage and hydrological regulation. However, changes in environmental factors—such as rainfall, groundwater levels, vegetation moisture, and land surface temperature—are often not immediately apparent.

While NASA provides decades of Earth observation data, accessing, comparing, and interpreting these datasets can be challenging for those without specialized expertise. Furthermore, it is easy to misinterpret a single month of unusually dry or hot weather as a long-term environmental trend.

This issue is particularly relevant in Sarawak. According to two news reports released by the Sarawak Public Communications Unit (UKAS) in 2026, the Sarawak government is intensifying its monitoring and prevention efforts regarding haze and peatland fire risks—including the use of drones for surveillance—with Kuala Baram identified as a high-priority area for peatland fire risk. [1][2]

PeatLens aims to provide a more intuitive, science-based approach to understanding environmental changes in peatlands, allowing users to explore the direction, magnitude, and statistical significance of these shifts based on historical data.

3. Our Solution

PeatLens offers an interactive platform that integrates geographical exploration, environmental education, and historical trend analysis.

To begin, users can explore the study area in Kuala Baram via an interactive map. The website also provides schematic diagrams of peatland profiles, helping users understand the relationships between rainfall, peat soil, and model-estimated groundwater levels.

Furthermore, users can explore historical NASA observational data through interactive time-series charts, allowing them to select specific analysis periods and examine fluctuations in environmental indicators across different months.

The platform integrates a variety of environmental datasets including rainfall, land surface temperature, vegetation indices, proxies for vegetation moisture, and model-estimated groundwater levels—enabling users to compare different environmental factors within a single, unified interface.

In addition, PeatLens employs the "Seasonal Mann–Kendall Test" and "Sen’s Slope Estimate" to provide statistical evidence, helping users determine the direction and magnitude of changes in environmental indicators, as well as whether these trends are statistically significant.

The website also incorporates historical thermal anomaly records from NASA FIRMS as supplementary background information; however, these observations are not equated directly to individual fire events, nor are they used to infer causal relationships between environmental changes and fires.

4. Development Process

The development of PeatLens integrates AI-assisted software engineering, Earth observation data processing, and modern web development technologies.

Throughout the development lifecycle, we utilized "Kiro AI Agents" to assist with project planning, coding, code review, debugging, and testing, thereby enhancing development efficiency and supporting tasks related to data integration and software engineering.

For Earth observation data processing, we leveraged "Google Earth Engine" (GEE) and its JavaScript API to filter NASA satellite data for our study areas, perform quality control, conduct spatial statistical aggregation, and export monthly time-series datasets.

Additionally, we utilized a local "Python" environment to organize the exported environmental data, perform trend analysis, and verify the results.

The website is built using modern JavaScript web development technologies, with "Vite" employed for both development and the build process. The source code is managed through Git and GitHub, and the project is deployed as a publicly accessible static research website using GitHub Pages.

Rather than relying on physical environmental sensors installed on-site, this project utilizes existing NASA Earth observation data to conduct historical environmental investigations.

5. Benefits & Impact

PeatLens aims to make it easier for students, educators, environmental researchers, and local stakeholders to explore and understand NASA Earth observation data.

By integrating various environmental indicators, interactive charts, and statistical results, the website lowers the barrier to using Earth science data, enabling users to gain a more evidence-based understanding of environmental changes.

In an educational context, PeatLens helps students grasp the interconnections within Earth systems, as well as the distinctions between short-term environmental fluctuations and long-term trends.

Regarding environmental research and public awareness, the project provides supporting information for exploratory studies on peatland changes, environmental education, and related discussions.

By using Kuala Baram as an initial case study, the project bridges the gap between global NASA Earth observation data and local environmental issues in Sarawak.

6. Limitations & Future Development

PeatLens is currently an early-stage research and educational prototype, focused primarily on the Kuala Baram region and utilizing a limited set of environmental indicators to examine historical trends.

Due to variations across NASA datasets—such as differences in spatial resolution, temporal coverage, data completeness, and measurement methodologies—some indicators serve only as indirect proxies for actual environmental conditions. For instance, the vegetation moisture index is a remote-sensing proxy, while groundwater level data are model-based estimates rather than direct field measurements. Currently, static data files such as CSVs require manual updates. Future versions could automate data processing and updates through scheduled workflows using the Google Earth Engine (GEE) API.

Additionally, the current statistical analysis is primarily intended for exploring historical trends; some methods for assessing uncertainty still require further review and validation.

In the future, with access to more comprehensive environmental data, field observations, and more robust validation criteria, the PeatLens research framework could be extended to other peatland regions, enabling further investigation of relationships among environmental indicators.

It should be emphasized that PeatLens is not a real-time fire early-warning or prediction system; rather, it serves as a scientific research and educational tool designed to help users understand long-term environmental changes.

7. Creativity & Innovation

The innovation of PeatLens lies in its integration of multi-source NASA Earth observation data, scientific statistical analysis, and interactive environmental education, creating a platform that enables non-specialist users to investigate environmental trends in peatlands.

i) Integration and comparison of multiple indicators.

Moving beyond single metrics like temperature or rainfall, PeatLens synthesizes diverse environmental data—including precipitation, land surface temperature, vegetation indices, proxies for vegetation moisture, and model-estimated groundwater levels. This allows users to explore and compare the historical evolution of multiple Earth system variables within a single platform.

ii) Combining trend visualization with statistical evidence.

While it is easy for the average user to interpret the rise or fall of a line on a graph as environmental change, such visual shifts do not necessarily represent long-term trends with statistical significance.

PeatLens pairs interactive time-series charts with the Seasonal Mann–Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimate, enabling users to understand the direction, magnitude, and statistical significance of trends, rather than relying solely on superficial visual observations.

iii) Interactive scientific storytelling.

PeatLens goes beyond merely providing data charts; it offers a structured, step-by-step environmental investigation experience.

Users can begin by exploring a map, gain an understanding of the ecosystem through schematic diagrams of peatland profiles, and subsequently delve into historical data analysis and the interpretation of scientific findings.

This progression from geographic awareness to scientific inquiry—makes complex Earth observation data more intuitive and accessible, while fostering greater user interest in environmental research.

iv) Bridging local environmental issues with global scientific data.

PeatLens features the Kuala Baram peatland region as its initial case study, connecting global NASA Earth observation data with environmental issues of local relevance in Sarawak.

At the same time, the project prioritizes transparency in scientific interpretation, clearly distinguishing between observational data, indirect proxy indicators, model estimates, and statistical inferences to ensuring that correlation is not mistaken for causation.

The innovation of PeatLens does not lie in the creation of entirely new satellite data or statistical methods; rather, it integrates existing scientific resources into an experience that makes investigating environmental trends easier to explore, understand, and apply.
